unit.title: Develop and implement work unit plan

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: A section head in a ministry is writing her unit's plan for the coming year. What should the plan be built on first?

essays.stem: You head the customer service unit of a government agency. Plan the steps you would take to develop your unit's work plan for the next financial year.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start with the agency's strategic and corporate plans to see which goals my unit must support, such as faster service and more online transactions, and I would check the budget ceiling and any new policy directions. I would review last year's results, customer feedback and complaints to see where we fell short. Next I would hold a planning session with my team, because they know the work and will deliver it. Together we would set three to five SMART objectives, for example 'answer 90% of calls within two minutes by March'. For each objective we would list the activities, who leads each one, start and end dates and milestones, shown on a Gantt chart. I would work out the resources needed: staff hours compared with the workload, equipment, training and a budget in J$. I would identify risks, such as staff shortages or system failures, with responses, and set performance measures and how data will be collected. I would agree support needed from other units, then submit the plan to the director for approval and brief the team once it is approved.
markingPoints: Links the plan to corporate priorities and reviews past results and feedback
Involves the team in setting SMART objectives
Plans activities, responsibilities, timelines and milestones
Works out resources, budget, risks and measures
Coordinates with other units, gets approval and communicates the plan

essays.stem: Explain how a manager should write objectives and performance measures for a public service unit, and why measuring outcomes as well as outputs matters.
essays.modelAnswer: Objectives should be SMART: specific about what will change, measurable, achievable with the resources available, relevant to the agency's goals, and time-bound. For example, 'reduce the average time to issue a birth certificate from 15 to 7 working days by December' is far clearer than 'improve service'. Each objective should have one or two performance measures, with a baseline, a target and a clear definition, so everyone counts in the same way. Measures should rely on data that can be collected easily as the work is done. Outputs are the things a unit produces, such as the number of certificates issued or workshops held. They are useful for managing workload, but they do not show whether the public is better off. Outcomes are the results for citizens, such as shorter waiting times, higher satisfaction or fewer repeat visits. A unit could hold many workshops and still achieve little, so measuring outcomes keeps attention on the purpose of the work. A good plan therefore uses a mix: outputs to track activity and outcomes to judge success, and reviews both regularly.
markingPoints: Explains each part of a SMART objective
Gives a relevant example of a well-written objective
Says measures need baselines, targets, definitions and practical data
Explains the difference between outputs and outcomes
Explains why outcomes matter and recommends a mix

essays.stem: A permits unit has 7 officers, each with 1,600 productive hours a year. Next year it expects 4,000 applications, each taking 2.5 hours, plus 1,800 hours of community outreach. Calculate the capacity, the workload and any gap. Then compare two options to close the gap: overtime at J$1,800 an hour, or a temporary officer for six months at J$1,350,000 who would give about 800 productive hours. Recommend one.
essays.modelAnswer: Capacity is 7 × 1,600 = 11,200 hours. The workload is 4,000 × 2.5 = 10,000 hours for applications plus 1,800 hours of outreach, a total of 11,800 hours. The gap is 11,800 − 11,200 = 600 hours. Overtime to cover 600 hours would cost 600 × J$1,800 = J$1,080,000. The temporary officer would cost J$1,350,000 and give about 800 hours, which covers the gap with 200 hours to spare, at about J$1,688 per hour. Overtime is J$270,000 cheaper in total and needs no recruitment, but it adds to the workload of officers who are already fully booked, which can lead to tiredness, errors and stress, and depends on staff agreeing to it. The temporary officer costs more but gives spare capacity for busy periods or sick leave, and protects staff wellbeing, although recruiting and training takes time. I would recommend the temporary officer if the budget allows, because the extra 200 hours give a safety margin and reduce the risk of burnout. If funds are tight, a smaller amount of overtime spread fairly could be used, while looking for ways to cut the time per application.
markingPoints: Calculates capacity of 11,200 hours and workload of 11,800 hours
Identifies the 600-hour gap
Calculates the overtime cost of J$1,080,000 and compares it with J$1,350,000
Weighs cost against workload, wellbeing, spare capacity and recruitment time
Makes a clear, justified recommendation

essays.stem: Your work unit plan has been approved. Describe how you would implement it during the first three months.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start with a team meeting to explain the approved plan, why it matters and how it links to the agency's goals, and to answer questions. Each officer would then agree an individual work plan with me, showing their tasks, targets and dates from the unit plan, and any training they need. I would make sure resources are in place: equipment working, budget released, vehicles booked for field work and access to systems arranged. I would confirm the support agreed with other units, such as finance and IT, and set dates with them. A simple tracking sheet would record progress on each activity, and I would explain how and when data must be entered. I would hold short weekly check-ins and a monthly progress review with the team, so problems surface early. During this period I would coach new or struggling officers, deal with blockages quickly and keep the director informed with a short monthly report. I would also recognise early successes to build momentum and adjust the timing of tasks where needed, with approval for any major change.
markingPoints: Briefs the team on the plan and its purpose
Agrees individual work plans and training needs
Puts resources and support from other units in place
Sets up tracking and regular check-ins and reviews
Coaches staff, reports to the director and adjusts with approval

essays.stem: Explain how you would monitor progress against a work unit plan and what you would do when results fall behind.
essays.modelAnswer: I would set up a simple monitoring system using the measures in the plan. Data would be recorded as the work is done, for example in a shared spreadsheet that logs cases received, completed and the time taken, so figures are reliable and up to date. Each month I would compare actual results with the monthly targets and milestones, and check spending against the budget. A one-page summary with red, amber and green ratings would show the position clearly. I would discuss the results at a monthly team review and send a short report to the director. When results fall behind, I would first find out why by talking with the officers involved and looking at the data: the cause might be staff absence, a system problem, more work than expected or a skills gap. Then I would agree corrective action, such as moving staff, coaching, fixing a process, seeking help from another unit or, if the target is no longer realistic, asking the director to approve a change. I would set a date to check whether the action worked and keep the team informed.
markingPoints: Uses the plan's measures and collects data as work is done
Compares actual with targets, milestones and budget regularly
Reports clearly to the team and the director
Finds the causes of shortfalls before acting
Agrees corrective action, seeks approval for target changes and checks results

essays.stem: Identify the main risks to delivering a work unit plan in a municipal corporation office, and explain how the plan should deal with them.
essays.modelAnswer: One risk is staff shortage through vacancies, sickness or leave. The plan should schedule work around known leave, train officers to cover each other's key tasks and note which tasks can be delayed. A second risk is a natural hazard such as a hurricane or flooding, which can close the office or create urgent extra work. The plan should include a contingency plan: back-up of records, a way to work from another location and an agreed list of essential services. A third risk is technology failure, such as a system being down or a new system arriving late. The plan should state its assumptions about systems, have manual back-up procedures and agree dates with the IT unit. A fourth risk is budget cuts or late release of funds, which the plan can address by ranking activities so lower priorities are dropped first. A fifth risk is new priorities from the council or the ministry. Each risk should be rated for likelihood and impact, given an owner and reviewed monthly, so that the manager can act early rather than react when it is too late.
markingPoints: Identifies staff shortage and how to plan for it
Identifies natural hazards and a contingency plan
Identifies technology or dependency risks and responses
Identifies budget or priority changes and ranking of activities
Explains rating, ownership and regular review of risks

essays.stem: Evaluate the benefits and difficulties of involving the whole team in developing a work unit plan, and explain how a manager can do it well.
essays.modelAnswer: Involving the team brings real benefits. Officers know the daily work, the time tasks really take and the problems customers face, so the plan is more realistic. People who help shape a plan understand it better and are more committed to delivering it, and good ideas often come from front-line staff. It also helps the manager spot skills and development needs. There are difficulties too. It takes time away from service delivery, some staff may push for low targets or their own preferences, louder members may dominate, and expectations can rise if staff think everything they suggest will be adopted. A manager can do it well by explaining the limits at the start, such as the corporate priorities and the budget, and being clear that she will make the final proposal. She can share the data in advance, use a structured session with a clear agenda, and give everyone a chance to contribute, for example through small groups or written ideas. She should explain afterwards which suggestions were used and why others were not. Overall, the benefits usually outweigh the costs if the process is well managed.
markingPoints: Explains benefits such as realism, commitment and ideas
Explains difficulties such as time, low targets and dominant voices
Sets limits and decision rights at the start
Uses a structured, inclusive process
Gives feedback on suggestions and reaches a balanced judgement

essays.stem: Six months into the year, the ministry directs your unit to take on a new national registration drive that was not in your plan. Explain how you would revise and implement the work unit plan.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first get the details of the new task: what is expected, the deadline, the targets and whether extra staff or money come with it. I would then estimate the workload in staff hours and compare it with the time left after the existing work. If there is a gap, I would rank the existing activities by priority and identify which can be delayed, reduced or stopped, and what extra resources are needed. I would discuss this with my team to check the estimates and hear their ideas. Next I would prepare a revised plan showing the new activities, the changes to existing work, the resources, the revised targets and the new risks, and present it to the director for approval, making clear what will not be done or will be late. Once approved, I would brief the team, update individual work plans, tell customers and other units about any changes to service, and update the monitoring sheet. I would watch staff workload and wellbeing closely during the drive and report progress on both the new and the existing work each month.
markingPoints: Clarifies the new task, deadline, targets and resources
Estimates workload and compares it with capacity
Reprioritises existing work and consults the team
Gets approval for a revised plan that states the trade-offs
Communicates changes, updates plans and monitors workload and progress

essays.stem: Describe how you would evaluate your work unit plan at the end of the year and use the results to improve next year's plan.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by comparing the year's results with each objective and measure: which targets were met, partly met or missed, and by how much. I would review spending against the budget and the staff hours used against the plan. I would gather other evidence, such as customer feedback, complaints, and comments from other units that depend on us. Then I would hold a review session with the team to discuss what worked, what did not and why, for example whether targets were set too high, a system came late or a new process saved time. I would look at whether the risks we identified happened and whether our responses worked, and note any risks we missed. The findings would go into a short evaluation report for the director, with lessons learned and recommendations. For next year, I would use these lessons to set more realistic targets, change how work is organised, plan training, ask for resources where the case is strong and improve the measures. I would also recognise the team's achievements, because this builds commitment for the next plan.
markingPoints: Compares results with objectives, measures, budget and hours
Gathers feedback from customers and other units
Reviews with the team what worked and why
Reviews risks and reports lessons to the director
Uses lessons to improve the next plan and recognises the team

essays.stem: Compare a work unit plan with a project plan, and explain how a manager should link the two when a unit runs a project alongside its normal work.
essays.modelAnswer: A work unit plan covers a unit's continuing work for a period, usually a financial year. It sets objectives linked to the corporate plan, the regular services the unit provides, staff and budget, measures and risks. A project plan covers a one-off piece of work with a clear start and end, a defined scope and deliverables, such as setting up an online booking system. It has its own schedule, budget, risks and often a project team drawn from several units. The main differences are that a unit plan is ongoing and covers routine services, while a project is temporary and aims to create something new. When a unit runs a project alongside its normal work, the manager should show the project in the unit plan as a key activity, with its milestones and the staff time it needs, so that the effect on normal services is clear. Staff hours for both must be planned together to avoid overloading people. Progress on the project should be reported in the unit's monthly reports, and risks that affect both, such as key staff leaving, should be managed together.
markingPoints: Describes a work unit plan accurately
Describes a project plan accurately
Explains the main differences
Shows the project in the unit plan and plans staff hours together
Links reporting and risk management for both

practical1.title: Develop a work unit plan for a public service unit
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a made-up case pack for a unit in a public body, such as the records unit of a municipal corporation or the customer service unit of an agency. It includes an extract from the corporate plan, last year's results, customer feedback, a staff list with productive hours, the expected workload and the budget ceiling. As a group, write a work unit plan for the next financial year. Each member has a named role: objectives lead (links the plan to the corporate plan and writes three to five SMART objectives with measures, baselines and targets); scheduler (lists the activities with owners, dates and milestones and draws a Gantt chart); resources analyst (builds a spreadsheet comparing staff capacity with workload, works out any gap and drafts the budget in J$, checking every figure twice); risk officer (writes a risk table with at least five risks, ratings, owners and responses, and states the key assumptions); and plan editor (writes the unit's purpose, puts the plan together and prepares a one-page summary for the director). In a group of four, the plan editor also writes the risk table. Every member presents their part to the assessor, who plays the director approving the plan.
materials: Computers with word processing and spreadsheet software
Work unit plan, Gantt chart and risk table templates
Printer, paper, flipchart paper and markers
photos: The SMART objectives with measures and targets
The capacity and budget spreadsheet on screen
The risk table and key assumptions
The finished plan and the one-page summary
The group presenting to the assessor
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the plan
Objectives are SMART and clearly linked to the corporate plan
Activities have owners, dates and milestones
Capacity, workload, gap and budget are calculated correctly and were checked twice
Risks have ratings, owners and responses, and assumptions are stated
The plan is clear, complete and ready for approval
Presented their part clearly and answered the assessor's questions
safety: Treat the case pack as confidential; return it to the assessor
Use made-up staff names only and no real personal information
Plan workloads that are fair and safe, with no unrealistic overtime
Share the workload fairly and take a short screen break each hour

practical2.title: Run a quarterly progress review and revise the unit plan
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a made-up work unit plan and the first quarter's results, which show some targets met and some missed, an overspend on one budget line and a new instruction from the director. Part A (45 minutes): analyse the results. Part B (40 minutes): hold a progress review meeting of the unit, then Part C (45 minutes): write the outputs. Each member has a named role: unit manager (chairs the review meeting, leads the discussion of causes and agrees corrective actions); performance analyst (builds a spreadsheet of targets against results, works out percentages and the budget variance, checking every figure twice, and presents them); team officer (explains the causes of one missed target from a role card and suggests a fix); planning officer (revises the plan and Gantt chart to fit the director's instruction, showing what will be delayed); and recorder (writes the meeting notes and the action list). In a group of four, the unit manager also records the actions. After the meeting, the group writes a one-page progress report to the director with a request for approval of the changes, the revised plan pages and two updated individual work plans. Every member writes or checks part of these documents.
materials: Work unit plan, first-quarter results and the director's instruction from the assessor
Computers with spreadsheet and word processing software
Progress report, meeting notes and individual work plan templates
photos: The results spreadsheet on screen with percentages and the budget variance
The review meeting in progress (faces only if all agree)
The meeting notes and action list
The revised plan pages and Gantt chart
The progress report to the director and the updated individual work plans
checklist: Took a named role and carried it out
Percentages and the budget variance are calculated correctly and were checked twice
Causes were found before corrective actions were agreed
Corrective actions have owners and dates
The revised plan shows clearly what changes and what is delayed
The progress report is clear and asks for the right approval
safety: Keep the results and notes confidential; return all papers to the assessor
Discuss performance respectfully: focus on the work, not on blaming people
Watch workload: revised plans must not rely on unsafe hours
Share the writing fairly and take a short break between parts
